proposals.imageObservation: Two open mid-pink five-petalled roses with yellow stamens and several slim buds at the top of a plate; the leaflets are long, narrow and finely toothed, willow-like; the stems are smooth, brown-purple to grey and carry no visible prickles; a small orange-red hip is drawn at lower left.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Both findings are colour adjectives, and the c82.net text (which is presumably where they came from, translating Thory) could not be fetched, so it is possible Thory wrote 'verts' and the colourist departed from him. Low-stakes either way. The plate number in the file URL (roses-035) matches Les Roses pl. 35, sold as 'Marsh Rose' (Rosa palustris / hudsoniana), which corroborates the identification.

proposals.title: Rosa Hudsoniana
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa hudsoniana subcorymbosa, a Hudson rose of two or three feet with thornless reddish branches and elliptical leaflets, green above and glaucous beneath. Its flowers gather in a loose corymb and show five or six ranks of soft pink petals around a sessile head of stigmas. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa hudsoniana subcorymbosa, a Hudson rose of two or three feet with thornless green branches and elliptical leaflets, green above and glaucous beneath. Its flowers gather in a loose corymb, a soft pink bloom beside a deeper crimson one, several ranks of petals around a sessile head of stigmas. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.

issues.quote: thornless reddish branches
issues.problem: The stems in the plate are green, not reddish.
issues.evidence: image - main stem and branchlets are pale green

issues.quote: five or six ranks of soft pink petals
issues.problem: Only the left-hand bloom is soft pink; the cluster also contains a distinctly deep crimson double flower, which the description does not account for. The number of petal ranks cannot be verified from the plate.
issues.evidence: image - two clearly different flower colours in the same corymb

proposals.imageObservation: A loose cluster of blooms: one pale pink many-petalled flower, one deep crimson double flower, a small yellow-centred single, and several buds, on smooth green thornless stems with elliptical leaflets shown green above and pale grey-green beneath.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The printing-technique sentence is correct for Les Roses and was kept verbatim. Only branch colour and the single-colour reading of the corymb changed.

proposals.title: Rosa Indica Sertulata
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa indica sertulata, a bushy Bengal rose carrying five or six flowers together in a kind of bouquet, the petals white at the claw and tender pink at the tip. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa indica sertulata, a bushy Bengal rose carrying its flowers together in a kind of bouquet, the petals pale at the claw and deep carmine toward the tip; a hanging cluster fills the upper left while one flat-open bloom faces out at the right. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.

issues.quote: the petals white at the claw and tender pink at the tip
issues.problem: The pale base is right, but the outer part of the petals is a deep carmine-crimson, not 'tender pink'. As written the description implies a pale blush rose; the plate is strongly red.
issues.evidence: image — deep crimson blooms with pale petal bases

proposals.imageObservation: Deep crimson-carmine roses on a prickly stem: a hanging cluster of three or four blooms at the upper left and one flat, fully open flower at the right whose petals are pale, almost bluish-white at the base and strong carmine toward the edges; several buds; light green leaflets.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I dropped the specific 'five or six flowers together' count because the plate's cluster reads as three or four open blooms plus buds and I could not check Thory's text (c82.net unreachable); if the source says five or six, restoring it is fine. Volume 3 / 1824 matches the catalogue year.

proposals.title: rosa indica stelligera
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa indica stelligera, a Bengal rose with rose-pink bloom and toothed leaflets on a slender branching stem. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824; Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose Malmaison garden seeded the work.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa indica stelligera, a Bengal rose whose single deep-crimson flowers open around a white eye and a ring of yellow stamens, on a slender branching stem with toothed leaflets. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824; Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose Malmaison garden seeded the work.

issues.quote: rose-pink bloom
issues.problem: The flowers are a deep crimson/carmine red with a pale white centre, not rose-pink.
issues.evidence: image — both open flowers are painted in dark carmine with a distinct white eye around the yellow stamens.

proposals.imageObservation: Two open single roses of deep crimson-carmine with a white eye and yellow stamens, plus buds, on a slender branching stem with toothed leaflets and small red prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Only the colour phrase is changed; the volume/date and the Josephine sentence are preserved verbatim. Les Roses appeared in three folio volumes 1817-1824, so a 1824 third volume is consistent with the catalogue year.

proposals.title: Rosa Indica Vulgaris
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa indica vulgaris, the common Indian rose, with smooth green canes four to six feet tall, glossy leaflets and semi-double soft-pink flowers borne several together in a loose panicle. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied the plate.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa indica vulgaris, the common Indian rose, its green canes four to six feet tall and armed with stout curved red prickles, carrying glossy leaflets and full soft-pink flowers borne several together toward the ends of the branches. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied the plate.

issues.quote: smooth green canes four to six feet tall
issues.problem: Read on its own this says the canes are unarmed, and the plate's most conspicuous feature is a row of stout hooked red prickles down the main cane. Thory's text says 'green and smooth ... armed with strong, curved, reddish prickles' — the description kept the first half and dropped the second.
issues.evidence: image (prickles clearly drawn) + web:https://www.c82.net/redoute/flower/rosa-indica-vulgaris (Thory text, reached via search snippet)

issues.quote: semi-double soft-pink flowers
issues.problem: Thory does call them semi-double, but the flower Redoute actually drew is full and many-petalled, so the phrase reads as contradicted by the plate.
issues.evidence: image — the open bloom shows many overlapping ranks of petals and no visible stamens

proposals.imageObservation: One fully double, cabbage-like soft-pink rose with two smaller blooms and four buds; the main cane is green but carries a series of stout, hooked, red prickles, and the leaflets are broad and smooth-edged.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Not a fabrication — the wording tracks Thory closely. The fix is to restore the prickles he also records, and to describe the flower as the plate draws it. If the project prefers to mirror Thory verbatim, leaving 'semi-double' is defensible; the prickles are not.

proposals.title: Rosa Kamtchatica
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa kamtchatica, a two to three foot bush bristling with numerous straight whitish prickles, bearing large fragrant flowers of orange-red tinged violet and rounded red-brown hips. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's rose collection at Malmaison.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa kamtchatica, a two to three foot bush bristling with numerous straight whitish prickles, bearing a large single flower of deep carmine-pink around a ring of yellow stamens, with a rounded scarlet hip shown separately below. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's rose collection at Malmaison.

issues.quote: large fragrant flowers of orange-red tinged violet and rounded red-brown hips
issues.problem: The flower in the plate is a deep carmine or magenta pink, not orange-red, and the hip is bright scarlet, not red-brown.
issues.evidence: image - single bloom reads magenta-crimson; hip at lower left is clear red

proposals.imageObservation: A single large five-petalled rose in deep carmine-pink with a ring of yellow stamens, two buds, densely bristly stem with many straight pale prickles, greyish-green leaflets, and a separate bright scarlet rounded hip with sepals at lower left.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Height and fragrance are presumably from Thory's text and are unverifiable rather than wrong, so I left the height clause and dropped the unverifiable 'fragrant'. Only the colours were changed to match the plate.

proposals.title: Rosa Longifolia
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa longifolia, the peach-leaved rose, with long acuminate leaflets and ten to twelve uneven soft-pink petals sometimes flecked white, the inner ones crumpled and rolled at the centre, and an oval reddening hip. Thory's text reports it native to the East Indies, where its near-thornless stem grows tall.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa longifolia, the peach-leaved rose, with long acuminate leaflets and flowers of ten to twelve uneven soft-pink petals, some streaked white, opening flat around a ring of yellow stamens; the stem carries only a few small hooked prickles. The plate is from Redoute's Les Roses, with text by Claude-Antoine Thory.

issues.quote: the inner ones crumpled and rolled at the centre
issues.problem: The flowers are flat and open with the yellow stamens fully visible; there are no crumpled, rolled inner petals. The same phrase appears verbatim in this batch's Rosa muscosa description, which suggests it was carried over rather than observed.
issues.evidence: image - all three blooms show exposed stamens

issues.quote: an oval reddening hip
issues.problem: No reddening hip appears in the plate; the green structures behind the flowers are receptacles and buds.
issues.evidence: image

issues.quote: Thory's text reports it native to the East Indies
issues.problem: Range attributed to a source text that could not be fetched; Rosa longifolia is usually treated as a China-rose relative.
issues.evidence: c82.net blocked; knowledge

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: three pale-pink semi-double flowers of about ten uneven petals with whitish streaks, each showing a ring of yellow stamens at the open centre; long narrow willow-like leaflets and a few small hooked prickles on the stem. No ripe hip is depicted.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I dropped the crumpled-centre and reddening-hip details because the plate shows neither, and dropped the East Indies provenance because it rests entirely on a source I could not read. If Thory's text is recovered, the nativity line can go back as an attributed statement.

proposals.title: Rosa Lucida
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa lucida, the glossy rose, a thick bush five or six feet high with smooth canes and glossy leaflets, bearing light-pink flowers three or four together in terminal corymbs and flattened globular red hips. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses, published in 1817.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa lucida, the glossy rose, a thick bush five or six feet high with glossy leaflets and paired reddish prickles at the leaf nodes, bearing light-pink flowers three or four together in terminal corymbs and flattened globular red hips. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses, published in 1817.

issues.quote: smooth canes
issues.problem: The plate shows paired reddish prickles at each leaf node, drawn prominently. The canes are smooth between the nodes but are not unarmed, so a flat 'smooth canes' misleads.
issues.evidence: image - zoomed crop of the mid-stem shows clear infrastipular prickles

proposals.imageObservation: Two open single pink roses with yellow stamens and one bud on an arching stem, with glossy toothed leaflets in fives and sevens; paired reddish hooked prickles sit at the leaf nodes. A separate flattened globular red hip is figured at the lower left.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Small fix, optional. Everything else checks out: the hip at lower left is exactly the 'flattened globular red hip' described, the leaflets are glossy, and Les Roses volume one is 1817, matching the catalogue year and the plate number (roses-011).

proposals.title: Rosa Malmun­dariensis
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa malmundariensis, the Malmedy rose, a bush six or seven feet tall with mixed straight and hooked prickles and five very pale-pink petals notched at the heart, with large rounded red hips. Thory's text records that Dr Le Jeune found it on the mountains near Malmedy.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa malmundariensis, the Malmedy rose, a bush six or seven feet tall with mixed straight and hooked prickles and five pink petals notched at the heart, with large rounded hips shown still green. Thory's text records that Dr Le Jeune found it on the mountains near Malmedy.

issues.quote: with large rounded red hips
issues.problem: The hips in the plate are green, not red — they are drawn unripe.
issues.evidence: image — enlarged crop of the fruiting branch shows three or four olive-green rounded hips

issues.quote: five very pale-pink petals
issues.problem: The petals are a clear mid-pink, not "very pale".
issues.evidence: image — the open flower is a distinctly saturated pink against the white ground

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: a branching spray with one open five-petalled mid-pink flower notched at the petal tips, two small buds, and at the right a cluster of large rounded hips that are painted olive-green, each still crowned by spreading sepals; the main cane carries both straight and strongly hooked red prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The Lejeune / Malmedy attribution could not be verified (c82.net blocked) but is plausible: A. L. S. Lejeune was the Belgian botanist of the Verviers–Malmedy area, and malmundariensis is the Latin for Malmedy. I left that sentence untouched. The height in feet is likewise from Thory and unverifiable.

proposals.title: Rosa Muscosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa muscosa, the moss rose, a two to three foot bush with straight prickles, its stalks, hips and pinnatifid calyx lobes bristling with long glandular hairs that look like a mass of moss, the five-petalled light-pink flowers sweetly scented. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Roses, issued in 1817.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa muscosa, the moss rose, a two to three foot bush with straight prickles, its stalks, hips and pinnatifid calyx lobes bristling with long glandular hairs that look like a mass of moss, the sweetly scented light-pink flower opening in a single wide whorl of petals above two dark mossy buds. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Roses, issued in 1817.

issues.quote: the five-petalled light-pink flowers sweetly scented
issues.problem: The open flower in the plate carries a single whorl of about nine or ten petals, not five.
issues.evidence: image — enlarged crop of the bloom shows roughly nine to ten overlapping petals in one row

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: one wide-open light-pink rose with a single whorl of roughly nine or ten broad petals around a ring of yellow stamens, two deep-crimson buds whose receptacles and sepals are thick with green mossy glandular bristles, bristly flower stalks, a strongly prickled main cane and large blue-green leaflets.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Everything else holds: the mossy glandular bristles on stalks, receptacles and sepals are unmistakable in the plate, and Les Roses vol. 1 is 1817, matching the record year. Petal counting from a reproduction is the one soft spot — the count is clearly well above five, but I would not pin an exact number, so the replacement avoids one. Scent is not checkable from an image; it is standard for the moss rose and I left it.

proposals.title: rosa nivea
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa nivea, a thornless shrub barely two feet high with glossy three-part leaves and large, scentless, snow-white flowers about three inches across above pointed white buds. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa nivea, a rose Michaux collected in Georgia, with leaves mostly of three leaflets and large, scentless, snow-white flowers about three inches across above pointed buds. Prickles arm the lower stems. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied Redouté's plate.

issues.quote: a thornless shrub
issues.problem: The plant in the plate is conspicuously armed: red-brown prickles run along the main stem and the side branches.
issues.evidence: image — at least a dozen prickles are drawn on the stems

issues.quote: glossy three-part leaves
issues.problem: The leaves are pinnate with five or more leaflets and are painted matte, not trifoliate and glossy. The trifoliate, thornless, glossy-leaved plant is the Cherokee rose (the other plant that has gone under the name Rosa nivea), not the one drawn here.
issues.evidence: image — leaves throughout the plate carry two pairs of leaflets plus a terminal one

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: two open single white flowers with yellow stamens plus a white bud, on green stems that carry numerous stout red-brown prickles; the leaves are pinnate with five (sometimes more) matte green leaflets. White ground, no detail figures.
proposals.reviewerNotes: This looks like a description written from the botanical characters of a different plant that has carried the same name (Rosa laevigata / R. nivea DC., which is near-thornless with three glossy leaflets) rather than from the plate in hand. I dropped 'barely two feet high', 'scentless' and 'about three inches across' from the replacement — all unverifiable here, and c82.net (the source page with Thory's text) returns 403.

verifier.reason: Only half the finding holds. 'Thornless' contradicts the plate: I can see prickles on the lower main stem and side branches. But the claim was not imported from another plant. A search of the c82.net text shows Thory himself calls the stems thornless and barely two feet high, and says the leaves have three, rarely five, leaflets. That is also what the plate shows: most leaves carry three leaflets. The first agent's 'pinnate five-leaflet leaves' is wrong, and its replacement would add that error. The flower size, lack of scent and pointed white buds also come from Thory's text. So the one real problem is repeating a source claim that the picture contradicts. That is minor, not major. My corrected text keeps the grounded details, drops the unconfirmed 'glossy' and the misleading height, and notes the prickles.

proposals.title: Rosa Pimpinellifolia
proposals.currentDescription: A red double form of Rosa pimpinellifolia, a dense bush about a foot and a half high with rounded leaflets and soft-rose, lightly scented flowers, its small cherry-sized hips ripening from red to black. The corolla varies from five to seven rows of petals. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses (1817).
proposals.proposedDescription: A red double form of Rosa pimpinellifolia, a dense low bush with small rounded leaflets and soft-rose, lightly scented flowers, its small cherry-sized hips ripening from red to black. The corolla is semi-double, a few ranks of petals around an open boss of stamens. Redouté drew it for the first volume of Les Roses (1817).

issues.quote: The corolla varies from five to seven rows of petals.
issues.problem: The flowers as drawn are semi-double, with roughly two to four ranks of petals and the stamens plainly visible at the centre — not five to seven rows, which would hide the stamens entirely.
issues.evidence: image — the open flower at left shows an outer and an inner rank of petals around an exposed yellow stamen boss

issues.quote: a dense bush about a foot and a half high
issues.problem: A specific measurement that nothing available backs; presumably from Thory's text, which could not be fetched.
issues.evidence: c82.net unavailable (Cloudflare challenge); the image is a cut branch and says nothing about the plant's height

proposals.imageObservation: A densely thorned burnet-type rose with many small rounded leaflets, bearing four soft pink semi-double flowers with visible yellow stamens plus several buds, each seated on a dark, almost black rounded hip.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The blackening hips and the rounded leaflets both match the plate and the species, so the description is about the right rose. The petal-rank count is the one thing the image argues against; I dropped the height rather than keep an unverifiable figure, but if a human can reach Thory's text on c82.net and it gives both numbers, restore them and disregard this finding.

proposals.title: Rosa Pinpinellifolia Inermis
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa pimpinellifolia inermis, a thornless burnet rose to three feet bearing single five-petalled flowers that range from light to deeper red, above leaves of up to eleven rounded leaflets. The young branches carry a few prickles that vanish as they grow. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa pimpinellifolia inermis, a thornless burnet rose to three feet bearing single five-petalled flowers, white with the faintest pink flush, above leaves of up to eleven rounded leaflets. The young branches carry a few prickles that vanish as they grow. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.

issues.quote: that range from light to deeper red
issues.problem: The flowers in the plate are white to the palest blush pink, not red at any depth.
issues.evidence: image | all four open flowers are white with a yellow centre and only a faint pink tinge at the petal edges

proposals.imageObservation: Four open five-petalled flowers, white with the faintest pink flush and a broad yellow centre, on a smooth grey stem with many small rounded leaflets and several dark purple-black hips; no prickles are visible on the main stem.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Only the flower colour is wrong; everything else (thornless stems, many small rounded leaflets, the stipple technique) matches. The likely source of the error is a mistranslation of a French 'rose' (pink) in Thory's text. Kew records the name as published in Redoute & Thory, Roses 3: 23 (1821), while the record dates the plate 1824 - within the issue span of the third volume, so I did not raise it as a metadata issue.

proposals.title: Rosa Pumila
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa pumila, a German sub-shrub to about a foot and a half with firm five-part leaves and fragrant flowers of five large petals, whitish outside and light purple within, above pear-shaped hips that turn reddish or orange and persist through winter. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text for the plate.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa pumila, a German sub-shrub to about a foot and a half with firm five-part leaves and fragrant flowers of five large petals, whitish outside and light purple within. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text for the plate.

issues.quote: above pear-shaped hips that turn reddish or orange and persist through winter
issues.problem: Reads as a description of the plate, but no hips are shown: the sheet has flowers, buds, stems and leaves only.
issues.evidence: image - checked the whole lower half at 2x; only leaves, stems and one bud

proposals.imageObservation: Three single (five-petalled) rose flowers, magenta-pink with yellow stamens and paler reverses, plus two buds, on thorny stems with leaves of five toothed leaflets. No hips or fruit appear anywhere on the plate.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The hips claim may well be a true botanical fact lifted from Thory's species description, but as written it places them in the picture. If the intent was species botany rather than what the plate shows, it should be re-worded rather than deleted - I removed it because I cannot check the source (c82.net unreachable).

proposals.title: Rosa Rosenbergiana
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa rosenbergiana, a very bushy shrub to about three feet with yellowish prickles, oval crenate leaflets, and umbel-like clusters of many-petalled white flowers tinged rose at the centre. The turbinate calyx tubes bristle with small prickles like the branches. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa rosenbergiana, a very bushy shrub to about three feet with yellowish prickles, oval crenate leaflets, and umbel-like clusters of many-petalled white flowers flushed rose on the outer petals and at the bud tips. The turbinate calyx tubes bristle with small prickles like the branches. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.

issues.quote: white flowers tinged rose at the centre
issues.problem: The rose tinge sits on the outer petals and the bud tips; the centre of the open flower is white with yellow stamens.
issues.evidence: image — a 3x crop of the open bloom shows a pink streak on an outer right-hand petal and a pink flush at the base of the lower outer petals, with a clean white-and-yellow centre.

issues.quote: a very bushy shrub to about three feet
issues.problem: Habit and height cannot be judged from a plate that shows one branch; presumably from Thory's text, which I could not read.
issues.evidence: c82.net is bot-blocked and no transcription surfaced in search.

proposals.imageObservation: One open white rose of many petals, its outer petals streaked and flushed pink at the edges and a boss of yellow stamens at the centre, surrounded by a cluster of pink-tipped buds on turbinate ovaries; every stem, pedicel and ovary is densely covered with fine pale bristles; leaflets are oval and toothed.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Only the placement of the pink is changed. If Thory's original text happens to say the flowers are rose-tinted 'au centre', the plate still contradicts it, so the fix stands on the image. The bristly turbinate calyx tubes and the umbel-like cluster are both clearly visible and were left verbatim.

proposals.title: Rosa Rubiginosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa rubiginosa in a densely prickled form, its branches bristling with unequal straight spines below seven-leaflet foliage and small pale-pink five-petalled flowers borne in twos and threes. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa rubiginosa in a densely prickled form, its branches bristling with unequal straight spines below compound foliage and five-petalled flowers of pale to deep rose-pink borne in twos and threes. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.

issues.quote: small pale-pink five-petalled flowers
issues.problem: The blooms range from mid-pink to a distinctly deep rose-pink; the right-hand flower in the plate is saturated, not pale.
issues.evidence: image — three open flowers of noticeably different pink intensities

proposals.imageObservation: A rose with stems and branches densely armed with unequal straight bristles and spines, carrying a cluster of three open five-petalled flowers with yellow centres at the top plus several buds; the right-hand flower is a deep rose-pink, the two others a lighter pink.
proposals.reviewerNotes: This is a borderline colour nit and a reviewer could reasonably leave the original alone; everything else in the sentence (the dense unequal straight prickles, the flowers in twos and threes, Thory's authorship) is right. I also dropped 'seven-leaflet' from the replacement because leaf counts in the plate look mixed (five and seven both appear) and I could not count them reliably — but I did not raise it as an issue for the same reason.

proposals.title: Rosa Rubiginosa Vaillantiana
proposals.currentDescription: A sweetbriar variety, Rosa rubiginosa vaillantiana, its five-petalled flowers opening faintly washed with pink then settling to a pure matt white that lasts until the petals fall. This colour shift sets it apart from the redder roses of the rubiginosa group, which hold their hue to the end.
proposals.proposedDescription: A sweetbriar variety, Rosa rubiginosa vaillantiana, its five-petalled flowers opening faintly washed with pink then settling to a pure matt white that lasts until the petals fall. The plate shows three blooms open along an arching, hook-prickled cane above small doubly toothed leaflets.

issues.quote: This colour shift sets it apart from the redder roses of the rubiginosa group, which hold their hue to the end.
issues.problem: A specific comparative botanical assertion about the whole rubiginosa group holding their colour until the petals drop, with nothing in the image, the record or any reachable source behind it.
issues.evidence: image shows only this plant; c82.net source text unavailable; no reference found for the claim

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: a branching sweetbriar spray with three open five-petalled pure-white flowers with yellow centres, a couple of buds and one spent flower, small doubly toothed leaflets, and long canes armed with stout hooked red prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The white flowers and five petals are confirmed by the plate; the pink-then-white transition is not visible in a single plate and is presumably Thory's observation, so I kept it as-is rather than removing an unverifiable but plausible source claim. The removed sentence is the one that reads as invented generalisation. Low priority overall.

proposals.title: Rosa Rubrifolia
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa rubrifolia, a tall briar reddish and glaucous throughout, its flowers red in bud and opening to greenish-white in clustered heads above oval wine-tinted leaflets. Redoute drew it for Volume 1 of Les Roses, published in 1817.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa rubrifolia, a tall briar reddish and glaucous throughout, its flowers deep red in bud and opening rose-pink with white at the base of the petals, carried in clustered heads above oval wine-tinted leaflets. Redoute drew it for Volume 1 of Les Roses, published in 1817.

issues.quote: opening to greenish-white in clustered heads
issues.problem: The open flowers are clearly rose-pink with a white base to the petals; nothing in the plate is greenish-white.
issues.evidence: image — every open bloom is pink

proposals.imageObservation: A corymb of five or six open flowers with rose-pink petals that pale to white at the base around yellow stamens, plus a darker red half-open bud; the foliage is grey-green and glaucous, flushed pink and wine-red at the edges, on reddish-purple canes with stout curved prickles; a red-brown hip is drawn at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The rest of the sentence (reddish and glaucous throughout, red buds, clustered heads, wine-tinted leaflets) is exactly what the plate shows, so only the four words about the opened flower colour need replacing. The file URL (roses-004) is consistent with a Volume 1 plate and with the 1817 date in the record.

proposals.title: Rosa Sepium
proposals.currentDescription: A pink-flowered hedge rose, Rosa sepium, tall and branching with whitish hooked spines and small leaflets glandular beneath. The five petals open soft pink but lose colour and whiten within hours, especially in full sun, above smooth ovoid hips.
proposals.proposedDescription: A pink-flowered hedge rose, Rosa sepium, tall and branching with whitish hooked spines and small leaflets glandular beneath. The five petals open soft pink but lose colour and whiten within hours, especially in full sun - the plate shows one flower still pink and another already almost white.

issues.quote: above smooth ovoid hips
issues.problem: No hips appear on the plate; the sentence is placed as a description of what is shown.
issues.evidence: image.

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: a tall arching hedge rose with two open five-petalled flowers - one pale pink, one nearly white with a pink edge - a pink bud, whitish hooked prickles, and many small serrated leaflets. No hips are depicted.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The fading claim could not be checked against Thory (c82.net blocked), but it is consistent with the plate, which figures the same species at two stages, so it was kept. Only the undepicted hips were dropped.

proposals.title: Rosa Tomentosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, its leaflets clothed both sides with soft pressed hairs and its pale-pink flowers above elongated ovoid hips. Josephine Redoute discovered it near Paris in the woods of Meudon in 1817, where it had escaped earlier botanists.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, its leaflets clothed both sides with soft pressed hairs, a single white flower open above a cluster of green ovoid buds, the cane armed with stout hooked prickles. Redoute found the rose in the woods of Meudon near Paris in 1817; Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the accompanying text for Les Roses.

issues.quote: Josephine Redoute discovered it near Paris in the woods of Meudon in 1817
issues.problem: The finder was Pierre-Joseph Redoute himself, who lived at Meudon; 'Josephine Redoute' conflates him with the Empress Josephine, his patron. The date and place otherwise match.
issues.evidence: web:https://aradergalleries.com/products/pierre-joseph-redoute-belgian-1759-1840 - Rosa tomentosa was discovered by Redoute near his home in Meudon in 1817

issues.quote: pale-pink flowers
issues.problem: The one open flower in the plate reads white with at most a faint blush; the buds are white with pink tips. Period text describing the species as pale pink may be the source of the wording.
issues.evidence: image

issues.quote: elongated ovoid hips
issues.problem: The plate shows green ovoid receptacles and buds, not ripe hips.
issues.evidence: image

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: a downy rose branch with a single open white flower (yellow stamens), one white bud opening and a cluster of green ovoid receptacles/buds, grey-green hairy leaflets and stout hooked red-brown prickles on the cane.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The Meudon/1817 discovery story is corroborated but belongs to Pierre-Joseph Redoute, not to anyone called Josephine Redoute - that is the finding worth acting on. Colour and hip wording tightened to what the plate actually shows.

proposals.title: Rosa Villosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa villosa in its turpentine-scented form, a bushy shrub bearing small five-petalled flowers that are red above and pale toward the base, set among large oval leaflets edged with sticky glandular hairs. The crushed foliage gives off a strong turpentine odour. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
proposals.proposedDescription: Rosa villosa in its turpentine-scented form, a bushy shrub bearing small five-petalled flowers that are deep pink toward the edges and pale toward the base, set among large oval leaflets edged with sticky glandular hairs. The crushed foliage gives off a strong turpentine odour. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.

issues.quote: flowers that are red above and pale toward the base
issues.problem: The petals are pink, deepest at the edges; "red" overstates the hue in the plate.
issues.evidence: image — the single open bloom is a mid rose-pink, comparable to the other Redouté pink roses in this batch

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: one open five-petalled flower, mid-pink deepening at the petal edges and paling to white toward the base around a yellow eye, with a cluster of buds beside it; large oval, sharply toothed leaflets and an arching stem with scattered red prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Petal count (five) and leaflet shape check out. The turpentine scent matches the epithet terebenthina and is not checkable from an image; the 1817–1824 publication span for Les Roses is correct. The colour call is the only finding and Thory's own French may well say "rouge", so treat it as low priority — medium confidence.

proposals.title: Rosa Indica
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa indica pannosa, the Bengal bichonne, a China cultivar under a foot and a half with concave frizzled petals of purple streaked in paler tones that give a marked cinnamon scent as they open. It was raised from seed about a dozen years earlier by Gauche, a Paris florist-gardener, who introduced it to foreign nurseries.

issues.quote: It was raised from seed about a dozen years earlier by Gauche, a Paris florist-gardener, who introduced it to foreign nurseries.
issues.problem: A named breeder and an origin story carrying the whole second sentence, with no backing in the image, the catalogue row, or any source I could reach. Web searches for a Parisian rose grower named Gauche in connection with the 'Bengale bichonne' returned nothing. This is exactly the shape a fabricated provenance takes - but it is also exactly the shape of a faithful paraphrase of Thory, and Thory's text is unreadable while c82.net is blocked.
issues.evidence: sourceEvidence note - c82.net behind a Cloudflare challenge; WebSearch for 'bichonne' + 'Gauche' found nothing either way

issues.quote: a marked cinnamon scent
issues.problem: Unverifiable sensory claim; same source problem.
issues.evidence: no accessible source

proposals.imageObservation: A China rose with two open double flowers - one cupped with crumpled, concave crimson-purple petals streaked paler, one flatter and deep crimson - plus several buds, red-tinted new shoots, mid-green leaflets and slender prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Do not act on this without reading Thory. The visual half of the description is unusually well matched to the plate - 'concave frizzled petals of purple streaked in paler tones' is precisely what the left-hand flower shows - which suggests the writer did have the source text in front of them, in which case the Gauche anecdote is probably a straight paraphrase. 'Bengale bichonne' as the vernacular name is confirmed by external listings of the plate. I am marking this unverifiable rather than major because I have no evidence the claim is wrong, only that nothing available supports it.

proposals.title: Blue Jay (Plate 102)
proposals.currentDescription: Plate 102 of Birds of America depicts three Blue Jays — labelled male, female, and a third — gathered on a leafy branch bearing tubular red and orange flowers. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell from Audubon's watercolour, the composition shows the vivid blue-and-white plumage and crested head of Cyanocitta cristata.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured folio plate: three blue jays with crested heads on a lichened branch bearing tubular red-and-orange flowers, one bird above pecking at a flower and two below, one of them holding a pale egg in its bill. Engraved caption reads 'Blue Jay. CORVUS CRISTATUS. Male 1. Female 2. 3.', with 'Drawn from nature by J.J. Audubon' at lower left and the Havell engraving line at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Count, plate number, engraver and species all confirmed by the plate's own lettering and the Commons record. The caption numbers the birds 'Male 1. Female 2. 3.', which the description's cautious 'male, female, and a third' handles correctly. One detail the description leaves out that would strengthen it: the lowest bird holds a stolen egg in its bill. Cyanocitta cristata is the current name for the plate's Corvus cristatus, so that is not an error.

proposals.title: Black & Yellow Warblers (Plate 123)
proposals.currentDescription: A study of magnolia warblers, formerly called black and yellow warblers, arranged on a flowering branch. Audubon's compositional habit of stacking multiple individuals across a single bough allowed him to display plumage variation within a species.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured folio plate: two warblers with yellow underparts streaked black, black-and-white wings and tails, perched on a bramble stem carrying pink five-petalled flowers, broad green leaves and clusters of unripe raspberries. Engraved caption at the foot names 'Black & Yellow Warbler'.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Species identification is confirmed by the Commons category 'Setophaga magnolia (illustrations)': the magnolia warbler was indeed published by Audubon as the black and yellow warbler. Two birds on a flowering-and-fruiting bramble matches 'multiple individuals across a single bough'. The generalisation about Audubon's compositional habit is a fair characterisation rather than an invented fact; the plant is a raspberry, which the description could have named.

proposals.title: Sharp-tailed Finch (Plate 149)
proposals.currentDescription: Three Sharp-tailed Finches are depicted in a marsh setting of grasses and reeds in Plate 149 of Birds of America: one bird sings from the tip of a bare twig, a second perches in the grass, and a third tends a nest at the base of the composition. The streaked breast and buff face pattern of the species are clearly rendered against the muted greens of the wetland vegetation. Audubon associated the species with the low coastal marshes of eastern North America.
proposals.imageObservation: A large sheet with wide margins carrying the plate: three streak-breasted sparrows with buff-orange face markings — one singing with open bill on a bare twig, one perched among grass blades at the right, one standing beside a woven grass nest at the base — set in coarse marsh grass with water and dark mud at the lower left. Plate CXLIX at upper right; caption 'Sharp-tailed Finch' below.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Count, postures, nest and habitat all check out on magnification, and the nest is correctly described as tended rather than as holding eggs (it is empty in the plate, so an eggs claim would have been the trap here). Plate number CXLIX = 149 is printed on the sheet. The Sharp-tailed Sparrow is a salt-marsh bird of the eastern North American coast, so the last sentence holds.

proposals.title: Louisiana Heron (Plate 217)
proposals.currentDescription: Tricolored heron, Egretta tricolor, captured in a sinuous wading pose with white belly stripe set against slate body. The dynamic curve of the neck typifies Audubon's preference for active, narrative postures over static specimen views.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured folio plate: a single heron on a log at the water's edge, neck curved down in an S, slate-blue body and wings, rufous-purple neck plumes, white line down the throat and white belly, long yellow-green legs; palmettos and swamp behind, engraved caption 'Louisiana Heron / ARDEA LUDOVICIANA / Male adult'.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Species identification (Egretta tricolor, Audubon's Louisiana Heron), the curved neck and the white underparts against a slate body all check out. The bird stands on a log rather than in the water, so 'wading pose' is a shade loose, but it is a wading bird in a characteristic attitude — not worth acting on.

proposals.title: Long-billed Curlew (Plate 231)
proposals.currentDescription: Two long-billed curlews stand among tall marsh reeds, their enormous decurved bills and cinnamon-buff plumage rendered at close range against a distant view of Charleston harbour. Audubon's use of a recognisable city skyline as backdrop is unusual for the series. Plate 231 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured folio plate: two long-billed curlews, one standing and one crouching, with very long decurved bills and cinnamon-buff barred plumage, on a rocky bank with tall marsh grass behind; across the water a low city skyline with spires and a fort under a cloudy sky; engraved caption ending 'City of Charleston'.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The Charleston claim is confirmed on the sheet itself — the engraved caption reads 'Long-billed Curlew. NUMENIUS LONGIROSTRIS. 1 Male 2 Female. City of Charleston' (read from a zoomed crop). Two birds, bills, plumage and the reed background all match. 'unusual for the series' is a soft generalisation but a fair one, and it is not doing load-bearing work.

proposals.title: American Snipe (Plate 243)
proposals.currentDescription: Three American snipe are shown on a muddy bank among reeds, with a riverside landscape visible behind. One bird stands alert with bill raised, while the others crouch low, their cryptic striped-and-barred plumage blending against the vegetation. Plate 243 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Male 1, Female 2, 3 and identified as Scolopax Wilsonii.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured aquatint plate: three snipe on a muddy bank among reeds - one standing upright with its long bill raised, one crouched behind it, one lying low at right; a river, distant trees and a house behind. Captioned 'American Snipe. Male 1. Female 2.3. / SCOLOPAX WILSONII'.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Counts, postures, setting and the printed caption all verified against the plate at magnification: the caption does read 'Male 1. Female 2.3.' and 'SCOLOPAX WILSONII'. The description avoids the leaked-field-name problem that its sibling Audubon entry in this batch has.

proposals.title: Manks Shearwater (Plate 295)
proposals.currentDescription: Plate 295 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a Manks Shearwater perched on the sea surface, dark brown-black above and white below, with a rocky coastal headland visible in the background. The species — a transatlantic pelagic seabird — is rendered in profile, its pale underparts contrasting sharply with the deep colouring of the back and wings.
proposals.imageObservation: Hand-coloured folio plate: one shearwater afloat in profile on a grey-green sea, blackish-brown above and white below, wings folded, pale feet trailing; low rocky headlands on both sides in the background; caption 'Manks Shearwater / PUFFINUS ANGLORUM'.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Plate number, species, plumage, profile and the background headlands all match the sheet. 'perched on the sea surface' is odd phrasing for a bird swimming, but it is not a factual error.

proposals.title: Pied Duck (Plate 332)
proposals.currentDescription: The Labrador Duck, extinct since around 1878, appears here in piebald drake plumage and brown female dress. Audubon's plate is now a historical document of one of the first North American birds lost to human pressure.

issues.quote: one of the first North American birds lost to human pressure
issues.problem: The cause of the Labrador Duck's extinction is genuinely unsettled - hunting, egging and the decline of its coastal shellfish food have all been proposed - so 'lost to human pressure' states more than is established.
issues.evidence: knowledge — the species' extinction cause is debated in the literature; the extinction itself and the c.1878 last record are not.

proposals.imageObservation: Two ducks on a rock at the water's edge under a pale evening sky: a pied black-and-white drake with raised wings and open bill, and a grey-brown female beside it, also calling. Caption 'Pied Duck. Fuligula Labradora.'
proposals.reviewerNotes: 'Pied Duck' is Audubon's name for the Labrador Duck, which the Commons category confirms (Camptorhynchus labradorius). The two plumages in the description match the plate. The extinction date of about 1878 is the standard last-record date. I would leave the text as it stands.

proposals.title: Snow Goose (Plate 381)
proposals.currentDescription: An adult white-morph Snow Goose stands beside a dark-morph (Blue Goose) individual, the latter showing a dark body with white head and neck, together contrasting the two recognised colour forms of the species. The black wingtips of the white bird and the pink bill and feet of both are rendered against a stormy coastal sky. Plate 381 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
proposals.imageObservation: Two geese on a sandy shore before green-blue sea and a heavy grey sky. The left bird is white with black primaries showing at the wingtip, a pink bill with a dark grin patch and bright pink legs and feet; the right bird has a clean white head and neck, a dark brown body, pale grey wing coverts, a pink bill and paler greyish-pink legs. Plate number and 'Snow Goose / Anser hyperboreus' engraved below.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The right-hand bird's clean white head with a dark brown body and pale grey coverts is the adult blue morph, so the description's reading is right. The Havell-edition span 1827-1838 and the University of Pittsburgh credit both come straight from the Commons record. One small stretch left alone: the blue morph's legs are a duller greyish-pink than the white bird's bright pink, so 'the pink bill and feet of both' flattens a real difference. The engraved caption line was too small to read at this resolution, so the plate's own labelling of the two birds could not be checked.

proposals.title: Ruffed Grouse (Plate 41)
proposals.currentDescription: Two male Ruffed Grouse fan their black-banded tails and erect their dark neck ruffs in courtship display while a female stands nearby amid dense foliage with large broad leaves and clusters of dark berries. Plate 41 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the species' dramatic sexual display within the leafy undergrowth of the eastern hardwood forest.
proposals.imageObservation: A hand-coloured aquatint plate with three Ruffed Grouse: one at the left and one at the upper right with tails fanned into banded discs and dark blue-black neck ruffs raised, and a third, plainer grey-brown bird standing at the centre front. Broad leaves, a trillium at the left, and clusters of dark berries fill the setting; the plate is numbered 'No. 9 / PLATE XLI' at the top and captioned 'Ruffed Grouse. TETRAO UMBELLUS Linn. Male 1.2. Female 3.' below.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I magnified the engraved caption to check the sexes: it reads 'Male 1.2. Female 3.', which confirms the description's two displaying males and one female. Plate number XLI matches 'Plate 41'. The berries, broad leaves and fanned banded tails are all present.

proposals.title: White-eyed Flycatcher or Vireo (Plate 63)
proposals.currentDescription: A single white-eyed vireo perches on a tall flowering plant in Plate 63 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the pale iris that gives the bird its name clearly visible beside a small spider rendered nearby. The botanical setting — a slender stem with delicate clustered blooms — gives the composition an airy openness quite different from the denser foliage of many plates. The title reflects the unsettled early-nineteenth-century taxonomy that grouped vireos among the flycatchers.
proposals.imageObservation: A large sheet with a wide blank margin; at its centre one olive-and-yellow vireo grips a slender stem head-downward, beak open, its pale iris clearly rendered, facing a small dark spider-like creature suspended to the right. The plant is a slim branching stem with small pink-white flower clusters and compound leaves. Engraved lettering below gives 'White-eyed Flycatcher or Vireo', 'Vireo Noveboracensis', the plate number and the plant name.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Checked at zoom: the pale iris is legible, and the small creature at the right does read as a spider (compact body with radiating legs) rather than a winged insect, so the description's most checkable visual claim holds. One nit I did not raise as a finding — the bird hangs head-downward with its beak open toward the spider rather than 'perching' in the ordinary sense; a rewrite could gain from saying so. The taxonomy sentence is a fair account of why the plate carries both names.

proposals.title: Rathbone Warbler (Plate 65)
proposals.currentDescription: A small warbler named in honour of the Rathbone family of Liverpool, patrons during the artist's English subscription drive. Now considered an immature or variant yellow warbler rather than a distinct species, the plate preserves a name otherwise lost from ornithology.

issues.quote: A small warbler named in honour of the Rathbone family of Liverpool
issues.problem: The description is entirely about the name and the taxonomy and never says what the plate shows - two birds, a male and a female, on a flowering honeysuckle vine.
issues.evidence: image + house style; the plate carries two birds, not one.

proposals.imageObservation: Two small yellow-olive warblers, one above and one below, perched on a trailing vine of red-and-yellow tubular honeysuckle flowers with dark green leaves, on a large cream sheet with an engraved caption.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Nothing in the text is false. The Rathbones of Liverpool did host Audubon during the 1826 English subscription drive and he named Sylvia rathbonia for them, and the bird is now treated as a yellow warbler - Commons files this plate under 'Setophaga aestiva (illustrations)'. Verdict kept at accurate per the rule that style issues do not lower it; a rewrite that opened on the two birds and the honeysuckle would fit house style better.

proposals.title: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus
proposals.currentDescription: A vehement Baroque mythology in which Castor and Pollux carry off the daughters of Leucippus, the rearing horses and twisting nudes locked into Rubens's signature swirling diagonal. Painted in Antwerp at the height of his powers, the picture exemplifies the warm, pearly flesh and muscular drama that defined his manner.

issues.quote: the picture exemplifies the warm, pearly flesh and muscular drama that defined his manner
issues.problem: Generic connoisseurial praise rather than information, though not inaccurate.
issues.evidence: image — the description of the flesh painting is at least borne out

proposals.imageObservation: A near-square canvas packed with figures: two nude women, one lifted up against a dark rearing horse by an armoured young man, the other sinking to the ground on gold drapery and held by a second bare-chested man in sandals; a grey horse rears at upper right, a winged putto steadies the dark horse at left, and a flat landscape and sky fill the remaining space.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Re-checked as if fresh. Subject (Castor and Pollux carrying off Leucippus's daughters), date 1618 and the Antwerp context are all standard and consistent with the Commons record. The canvas is in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich; the description does not name a collection at all, which is a gap rather than an error, and the record has no provenance to check against.

proposals.title: 1280px-Cypresses
proposals.currentDescription: A study of tall cypress trees by Vincent van Gogh, painted in 1889 during his time in southern France. The work exemplifies his distinctive swirling brushwork and vibrant palette in capturing the vertical forms and landscape. Part of the Metropolitan Museum of Art collection.

issues.quote: The work exemplifies his distinctive swirling brushwork and vibrant palette in capturing the vertical forms and landscape.
issues.problem: Generic catalogue filler; the crescent moon, the swirled sky, the blue hills and the flowering foreground are all left out.
issues.evidence: image

proposals.imageObservation: A tall dark-green cypress mass fills most of a vertical canvas, painted in thick curling strokes; behind it a turquoise sky with swirled clouds and a thin crescent moon at the upper right, blue hills at the right, and a foreground band of yellow-green grasses and small white flowers.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Date, place (southern France, 1889 — the Saint-Rémy year) and the Met provenance are all supported by the record's own wikidata provenance block and the Commons credit. Nothing contradicted; the description is merely vague.

proposals.title: The Bath of Psyche
proposals.currentDescription: Psyche stands nude beside a reflecting pool, drawing aside a length of drapery as she prepares to bathe, framed by two fluted columns. Leighton exhibited the oil at the Royal Academy in 1890; it was bought under the Chantrey Bequest and passed to the Tate. The narrow vertical format echoes a marble caryatid, the figure's weight set on one leg in contrapposto.
proposals.imageObservation: Tall narrow canvas: a nude woman stands on a stone step between two pale columns, lifting a length of translucent white drapery above and behind her head, with a terracotta jar and gold drapery at the right, a strip of cloudy sky above and her reflection in water at the bottom.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The pool (visible as reflection along the bottom), the drapery, the two columns and the standing nude are all in the frame. The Royal Academy 1890 exhibition, the Chantrey Bequest purchase and the Tate ownership are correct and consistent with the Commons date ('Exhibited 1890') and the 'Images from Tate Britain' category. The caryatid comparison and the contrapposto reading are interpretation, clearly marked as such.

proposals.title: 20. The Entrance Gate In Enoshima
proposals.currentDescription: Plate twenty of Hiroshige's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, showing pilgrims passing through the bronze torii at Enoshima with Fuji floating across Sagami Bay. The composition is built from flat overlapping silhouettes, a hallmark of late-Edo ukiyo-e landscape design.
proposals.imageObservation: Colour woodblock print, vertical: a large dark torii on the beach at Enoshima, three women in kimono with fans and a parasol in the foreground, small boats on the blue bay, a teahouse with awnings at left, and a snow-capped Fuji across the water; title cartouche upper right, artist's seal lower left.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Plate number, series, torii, Fuji across the bay and the flat overlapping design all match the print. Two small reservations, neither worth a finding: the three foreground figures are women travellers whose status as pilgrims is an inference (Enoshima was a pilgrimage site, so it is a fair one), and 'bronze torii' cannot be judged from the print's grey-black ink, though Enoshima's first torii was in fact bronze.

proposals.title: Fuji on the Left of Tokaido Road
proposals.currentDescription: Travellers move along the Tokaido highway as Mount Fuji rises to the left, a print from Hiroshige's posthumously published Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. The composition layers near figures against a flattened distance, exploiting the woodblock medium's graded skies and crisp silhouettes.
proposals.imageObservation: A vertical colour woodblock print: two travellers walk a yellow path in the foreground past the trunks of large pines, beyond them green paddy fields with figures and pack animals, and white-capped Mount Fuji rising at the left over red-lit hills; a graded blue sky at the top, two red cartouches (series title and print title) and the artist's red signature seal.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The cartouche reads 富士三十六景 (Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji) and 東海道左り不二 (Left Fuji on the Tokaido), matching both the title and the description. Hiroshige died in 1858 and the series was issued in 1858-59, so 'posthumously published' holds; the graded sky (bokashi) is plainly visible.

proposals.title: Study of an Old Woman
proposals.currentDescription: An oil sketch on oak panel of an elderly woman, made as preparatory study for figures populating Rubens's larger religious and mythological compositions. The loose, economical handling typifies the head-studies the Antwerp workshop produced from life models.

metadataIssues.evidence: commons imageDescription: 'Peter Paul Rubens, Studie van een oude vrouw, 1615-1620, olieverf op eiken paneel, 50,2 x 40,6 cm' - the record's 1610 is not supported by the source the record otherwise follows

proposals.imageObservation: Oil sketch: the head and shoulders of an old woman in a white headband, turned slightly to the viewer's left, with ruddy cheeks and heavy wrinkles, painted thinly and rapidly against a dark brown ground; a white collar stroke at the chest.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Medium, support and dimensions match the Commons description exactly (oil on oak panel, 50.2 x 40.6 cm - the record's realDimensions agree). The 'preparatory study for figures in larger compositions' reading is the standard account of Rubens's head studies and is consistent with the 'Tronies by Peter Paul Rubens' category. The date discrepancy is a record issue, not a description issue - the description gives no date.

proposals.title: Афганец
proposals.currentDescription: A standing portrait of an Afghan man in regional dress. Oil painting from Vereshchagin's Turkestan series, made in 1867 to 1868 after the artist joined General Kaufman's expedition to Central Asia. Vereshchagin combined ethnographic portraits of this kind with the battle scenes drawn from the same campaign.
proposals.imageObservation: Full-length oil portrait of a standing man in a white tunic and green-and-orange turban, a red sash holding pistols and a dagger, a striped shawl over one shoulder, a sabre at his side and a long musket held upright in his right hand; sunlit desert ground and a mud wall behind.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Commons gives 1867-1868 and the Turkestan series category; Vereshchagin did travel to Turkestan in 1867 at Kaufman's invitation. Nothing contradicted. The weapons - the most striking element of the picture - are not mentioned, which is an omission rather than an error.

proposals.title: View of Constantinople and the Bosphorus
proposals.currentDescription: Caïques and sailing ships line the Bosphorus shore at sunset, the quay busy with figures beneath a domed mosque flanked by twin minarets, the city's skyline of masts and minarets dissolving into golden haze beyond. Aivazovsky painted the view in 1856, drawing on visits to Constantinople in the 1840s and 1850s that made the Bosphorus panorama one of his recurring subjects.
proposals.imageObservation: A low sun over the water at the left throws a golden path across the strait; small caïques with rowers and passengers lie in the foreground, a large square-rigged ship is moored at a busy quay crowded with figures at the right, and a domed mosque with two tall minarets rises behind the quay, with a forest of masts and further minarets dissolving into golden haze up the shore.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Every visual element in the text is in the picture, including the twin minarets and the quay crowd. The 1856 date matches the Commons date field and the record. The travel claim is general ("visits to Constantinople in the 1840s and 1850s") and consistent with Aivazovsky's documented repeated visits from 1845 onward; it names no single trip, so it is not the kind of confident specific that would need a source.

proposals.title: Albinus
proposals.currentDescription: An engraving from Tabulae sceleti et musculorum corporis humani (Tables of the Skeleton and Muscles of the Human Body, 1747), the anatomical atlas of the Leiden anatomist Bernhard Siegfried Albinus, with plates drawn and engraved by Jan Wandelaar. The second table presents a full-length male ecorche displaying the superficial layer of muscles, posed with one arm extended before a parkland backdrop where a big cat watches from behind a masonry wall; Wandelaar's pictorial settings were meant to lend the figures depth and life. This impression is in the Wellcome Collection, London.

metadataIssues.proposed: Jan Wandelaar, after Bernhard Siegfried Albinus
metadataIssues.evidence: image | the engraved line at the lower left of the plate names Wandelaar as both draughtsman and engraver, and the running head names Albinus
knowledge | Tabulae sceleti et musculorum corporis humani was published at Leiden in 1747, the date the description itself gives

proposals.imageObservation: A full-length engraved écorché stands on a paved terrace with one arm hanging and the other extended sideways over a low stone wall; behind him a large cat rests its paws on that wall, with trees, a distant house and clouds beyond. Headed 'B.S.ALBINI' and 'MUSCULORUM TABULA II.', with engraver's and printer's lines along the bottom.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Everything checks against the plate: it is muscle table II, the figure is a full-length male écorché with one arm extended, the parkland setting and the big cat behind the masonry wall are there, and the Wellcome credit is in the record. Albinus's stated reason for the elaborate backgrounds (to give the figures relief and life) is standard. The plate is a muscle table rather than a skeleton table, which the description handles correctly by naming the whole atlas.

proposals.title: Praying Hands
proposals.currentDescription: A brush study in white and grey on blue prepared paper, drawn as a detail for an apostle in the Heller Altarpiece. The folded hands have since detached from their context to become one of the most reproduced devotional images in Western art.
proposals.imageObservation: A pair of hands pressed together in prayer, with a cuffed sleeve falling away at the right wrist, drawn in fine dark hatching and white heightening on paper prepared blue-green; the sheet's edges and a horizontal crease at the top are visible.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Support and technique match the sheet as reproduced (blue prepared paper, brush drawing with white heightening; the Albertina's own wording is grey and white ink on blue prepared ground, so 'white and grey' is faithful rather than an error). The Heller Altarpiece link is stated on the Commons record itself ('detail study for the Heller Altarpiece'). The provenance block already carries Albertina inv. 3113 and 19.7 x 29.1 cm, none of which the description contradicts. 'One of the most reproduced devotional images' is a superlative, but a very well-supported one, and I did not treat it as hype.

proposals.title: Alfons Much Slavnost svatovitova na rujane
proposals.currentDescription: A 1912 painting by Alphonse Mucha depicting the celebration of Svantovit (Svetovid), an ancient Slavic deity, in the context of Rujana. This work explores themes of spiritual salvation through art during times of conflict, reflecting Mucha's deep engagement with Slavic cultural and mythological subject matter.

issues.quote: This work explores themes of spiritual salvation through art during times of conflict, reflecting Mucha's deep engagement with Slavic cultural and mythological subject matter.
issues.problem: The description paraphrases the subtitle and the artist's general interests and never describes the crowd, the fires or the floating deities that fill the canvas.
issues.evidence: image — none of the depicted content is described.

proposals.imageObservation: A very large pale-toned canvas: a dense crowd in white robes gathers around fires and vessels in the lower half, while above them float visionary figures — a bearded god riding a beast among wolves and shields at the upper left, priests with staffs and ritual objects, and a leaping warrior — against a sky of blue and gold foliage.
proposals.reviewerNotes: No false assertion: 1912 matches Commons, Svantovit/Svetovid is correctly glossed as a Slavic deity, and Rujana (Rügen, with Cape Arkona in the Commons categories) is the right place. The description omits the single most useful fact — that this is one of the twenty canvases of Mucha's Slav Epic — which a rewrite should add; I did not write one because nothing is wrong.

proposals.title: Autumn
proposals.currentDescription: From the four-panel decorative series The Seasons, an allegorical figure reclines among grape vines, ripening clusters, and warm autumnal foliage, holding a shallow cup. The richly saturated ochre and burgundy palette and the sinuous interplay of figure and plant life are characteristic of Mucha's 1896 Seasons cycle.
proposals.imageObservation: A tall, narrow, round-cornered decorative panel: a long-haired woman in a pale gown leans back against a rock with one leg drawn up and one bare foot on the ground, holding a shallow white bowl, wearing a silvery chrysanthemum headdress. Dark grape clusters hang on a vine at the left with pink-orange maple leaves below, and a warm ochre-orange sky with bare branches fills the top. Signed at lower left.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Grape vines, ripening clusters, autumn foliage, the shallow cup and the warm ochre-and-burgundy palette are all in the panel, and the 1896 four-part Seasons series is correct and is echoed by the Commons categories. 'Reclines' is generous — she is seated and leaning back rather than lying — but it is a wording nit, not a false claim, so I left the verdict at accurate.

proposals.title: Winter
proposals.currentDescription: Closing the 1896 Seasons set, a woman wrapped in a flowing teal-green cloak cradles small birds against her chest among snow-laden branches. The warm amber background contrasted with the cold white snowfall and her verdant wrap demonstrates Mucha's command of decorative colour in this lithographic series.
proposals.imageObservation: A tall decorative panel: a woman in a pale teal-green robe drawn up over her head stands among snow-laden branches, cupping two small birds to her breast and breathing on them, against a warm amber ground with scrolling bare twigs.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Matches the image closely, including the teal wrap, the birds at her chest and the amber/white contrast. Winter is the last of Mucha's 1896 Seasons panels, so 'closing the set' holds. 'Cold white snowfall' is loose - the snow sits on the branches rather than falling - but too small to lower the verdict.

proposals.title: Kirche von Moret
proposals.currentDescription: The church of Notre-Dame at Moret-sur-Loing seen close up, its Gothic buttresses and stonework filling the upper canvas above a row of low houses. Sisley painted a series of views of the church between 1893 and 1894, varying the light across its west front. He worked the masonry in short strokes of cream, ochre and grey-blue.
proposals.imageObservation: A stone church seen close up and at an angle, filling most of the canvas: steep red-tiled roofs, turrets, buttresses with flying arches and a large traceried window, painted in short strokes of cream, ochre and grey-blue against a strong blue sky. Below to the right stands an open timber market hall with small figures under it; a street of low houses runs off at the lower left. Signed lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I initially read the depicted elevation as the apse and was ready to flag 'west front' — the account of the series is that the canvases show the church's west entrance and the south wall of the nave, all painted from an upstairs window opposite (web:https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moret_Church_(Sisley_series)), so the description's 'west front' stands and I withdrew the finding. The 1893-94 series dating and the handling of the masonry both check out. 'A row of low houses' is loose — most of what sits below the church is the market hall — but not false.

proposals.title: Überschwemmung in Port Marly
proposals.currentDescription: Floodwater standing in the streets of Port-Marly, a wine merchant's house rising from the inundated quay with a rowing boat alongside. Sisley returned to the flooded village several times in 1876, producing a small series of canvases of the high Seine.
proposals.imageObservation: A flooded street: a two-storey building at the left, its facade lettered 'A. ST NICOLAS' and, below, a longer sign, standing directly in brown floodwater; two boats with standing figures, a figure on a plank landing, half-submerged trees, lamp posts and a further boat with a shelter to the right, under a heavy grey sky. Signed 'Sisley 76' at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The wine merchant's house (the 'A. Saint-Nicolas' sign is legible in the image), the inundated quay and the boat alongside are all there, and Sisley's group of canvases of the 1876 Port-Marly flood is well established. Commons places this version in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen; the description makes no collection claim, so nothing to reconcile.

proposals.title: The Canal du Loing at Moret
proposals.currentDescription: The Canal du Loing at Moret recedes between rows of bare poplars whose trunks are doubled in the still water. Oil on canvas of 1892, given to the Musée du Luxembourg by friends of the painter led by Claude Monet after his death and now in the Musée d'Orsay (INV 20723). Sisley kept to the canal's straight perspective lines through many canvases of the early 1890s.
proposals.imageObservation: A canal running back into the distance under a pale, high sky, a row of bare poplars on the near towpath at the right and further trees beyond; white houses with dark roofs line the far bank at the left, with a moored barge and a small figure. The water carries clear vertical reflections. Signed and dated at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The provenance sentence is the risky one and it checks out: the picture was accepted by the State in 1899 as the gift of a group of Sisley's friends headed by Claude Monet for the Musee du Luxembourg, passed to the Louvre in 1929 and was assigned to the Musee d'Orsay in 1986, inventory INV 20723. I zoomed the water to test 'trunks are doubled in the still water': the canal does carry clear vertical reflections of the far bank and barge, so the phrase is defensible even though the near-bank poplars themselves are not obviously mirrored. Not enough to raise as a finding.

proposals.title: Women Going to the Woods
proposals.currentDescription: Figures on the main street of Marlotte, a village at the edge of the Fontainebleau forest, the women setting out to gather firewood. Oil on canvas, about 65 by 92 cm, painted in 1866. Sisley showed it at the Paris Salon that year, the first time the jury accepted his work.
proposals.imageObservation: A village street of stone houses with dark roofs; three women in shawls stand together in the middle of the road with other small figures beyond, one shifting brushwood at right. Signed and dated 1866 at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The Salon claim holds up: Sisley's 'Avenue of Chestnut Trees at La Celle-Saint-Cloud' was rejected in 1865 and the 1866 Salon catalogue lists this picture as 'Femmes allant au bois: paysage', so 1866 was his first acceptance. Dimensions of about 65 x 92 cm and the Artizon Museum (formerly Bridgestone) holding are corroborated. 'Main street of Marlotte' is the one soft detail - the picture is generally titled a village street in Marlotte, without 'main' - but it does not carry weight.

proposals.title: Allegorische voorstelling van het werk en de vlijt
proposals.currentDescription: Print depicting an allegorical representation of work and diligence. Created by Hendrick Goltzius.

issues.quote: Print depicting an allegorical representation of work and diligence.
issues.problem: The description is the Commons imageDescription verbatim and never says what is in the frame — the two lettered nude personifications, the tools, the visible date and signature.
issues.evidence: image | commons — the Commons imageDescription string is identical to the description, so no independent content was added.

proposals.imageObservation: An engraving of two muscular nude figures seated together on drapery, lettered 'Labor' (left, holding a spade shaft) and 'Diligentia' (right, holding a spindle or distaff on a cord); hammer, chisel, anvil and other tools lie in the foreground, the date '1582' at lower left and a 'Henricus Goltzius invent. et sculptor' inscription at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Nothing in the text is false: medium (print/engraving), subject (Labor and Diligentia), artist and 1582 date are all confirmed by the sheet itself, which carries the inscriptions. Style-only weakness; a rewrite would be a quality improvement, not a correction, so I left the verdict at accurate per the rubric.

proposals.title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival 清明上河圖
proposals.currentDescription: A Qing court reinterpretation of the celebrated Song handscroll documenting Qingming festivities along the Bian River. Shen Yuan, an academician under the Qianlong emperor, executes the panorama in fine ink line touched with sparing ochre washes.

issues.quote: an academician under the Qianlong emperor
issues.problem: The source says only 'an artist from the Painting Academy of the Qing imperial court' and 'fl. 18th century'; the specific reign attribution is an addition, though a conventional and likely one.
issues.evidence: commons imageDescription and artist field

proposals.imageObservation: The rendered file is a 960 x 27 pixel strip - an extremely long handscroll reduced to an unreadable band. At maximum zoom it resolves only as pale ground with fine grey ink detail of buildings, trees and figures, with no strong colour. Individual motifs cannot be made out.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I could not use the image - the rendered JPEG is 27 pixels tall - but the two substantive claims are lifted almost directly from the Commons record, which states that Shen Yuan was an artist of the Qing court Painting Academy and that this version is 'done mostly in ink with a few washes of ochre to the outlines'. That is exactly what the description says, so it stands on source evidence rather than on the image. Note the year field is null while the Commons date is 'Qing dynasty'.

proposals.title: Einzug des Kronprinzen Friedrich Wilhelm von Preußen in Jerusalem 1869
proposals.currentDescription: Wilhelm Gentz's monumental oil on canvas, more than two and a half meters wide, records the entry of Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm of Prussia, the future Emperor Frederick III, into Jerusalem in November 1869, a visit made on his journey to the opening of the Suez Canal. The prince rides a white horse at the center of a teeming procession outside the city walls, surrounded by dignitaries, onlookers in Ottoman and Arab dress and waving palm fronds, with the domes of Jerusalem beyond. Gentz, a specialist in Orientalist subjects, completed the painting in 1876, when it was acquired by the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.
proposals.imageObservation: Wide framed oil: a dense crowd outside the walls of Jerusalem, a rider in white robes on a white horse at the centre, palm trees and cut fronds, onlookers in Ottoman and Arab dress, mounted dignitaries and flags, the city walls and the Dome of the Rock in the background.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Checked: the Nationalgalerie record gives 131 x 258 cm (so 'more than two and a half meters wide' holds), 1876, and says the work was acquired by the Nationalgalerie before the 1876 Academy exhibition where it won a gold medal; the museum text also describes the entry as early November 1869 and the prince on a white horse. Sources: web:https://smb.museum-digital.de/object/144225.

proposals.title: Amor Vincet Omnia
proposals.currentDescription: A naturalistic Cupid in the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, who clambers grinning over scattered emblems of music, war, science, and rule. Caravaggio's tenebrist lighting and the boy's frank nudity made the picture notorious among Roman collectors.

metadataIssues.evidence: Commons imageDescription: 'Amor Vincit Omnia (c. 1601-1602), by Caravaggio. Oil on canvas, 156 cm x 113 cm. Gemaldegalerie, Berlin' - the description already names Caravaggio, so the null artist field is an internal gap in the record.
