proposals.currentDescription: A semi-double sweetbriar, Rosa rubiginosa, nursery-grown as the small Hesse rose, its tender-pink flowers carrying ten to twenty notched petals above apple-scented leaves. The orange-red hips stay nearly smooth at maturity and persist a long time.
proposals.imageObservation: A spreading briar with three open semi-double flowers of clear pink with yellow stamens, several buds and one spent flower, on green stems with scattered hooked prickles and small toothed leaflets; no ripe hips are shown.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The nursery name checks out: the plate's own text calls the shrub the 'rosier petite Hessoise', which is what 'the small Hesse rose' translates. Semi-double pink flowers and apple-scented (rusty, glandular) foliage match both the plate and that text. The hips are described but not depicted - the sentence reads as a statement about the plant rather than about the picture, so I did not treat it as contradicted, but a reader may expect to see them.

proposals.title: Rosa Sempervirens
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa sempervirens, the evergreen climbing rose, its stems reaching fifteen feet to clamber over shrubs and trees, with firm glossy leaflets and fragrant white five-petalled flowers in small clusters. The styles fuse into a short bristled column and the small round hips ripen red into winter.
proposals.imageObservation: A long arching prickly stem with a cluster of two open white five-petalled flowers with yellow stamens and one bud at the top, firm dark leaflets along the stem, and a separate study of a single red hip at lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: White five-petalled flowers in a small cluster, glossy firm leaflets and the red hip are all in the plate. The united (connate) styles forming a column are a real diagnostic character of R. sempervirens, and the fifteen-foot climbing habit and fragrance read as carried over from Thory's text — unverifiable from the image but not implausible or self-serving.

proposals.title: Rosa Sempervirens
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa sempervirens in a broad-leaved form, the evergreen climbing rose with its glossy persistent foliage and white flowers. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates throughout Les Roses.
proposals.imageObservation: One open white rose with yellow stamens at the top of an arching stem, with four buds; broad glossy leaflets and red-brown hooked prickles along the stem.
proposals.reviewerNotes: White flowers, broad glossy leaflets and the 'latifolia' (broad-leaved) form all match. Claude-Antoine Thory did write the descriptive text for Les Roses - correct. Style note only: the second sentence is generic series boilerplate that is reused verbatim-ish on the Rosa gallica entry in this same batch, and it says nothing about this plate.

proposals.title: Rosa Sepium
proposals.currentDescription: A near-double form of Rosa sepium, the hedge rose, its small spaced leaflets glandular beneath and four or five ranks of pale-red petals whitening toward the claw. The styles gather almost smooth in a bundle, and the ovoid calyx tube is hairless.
proposals.imageObservation: Pale pink near-double roses, two fully open and two in bud, on a long prickly stem with many small toothed leaflets; smooth green calyx tubes; plain white ground.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Petal colour, doubling and the small spaced leaflets match. The botanical particulars (glandular leaf undersides, bundled styles, hairless ovoid calyx tube) come from Thory's text and cannot be checked with c82.net blocked; the smooth calyx tubes are at least consistent with the plate.

proposals.title: Rosa Sepium
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa sepium in a myrtle-leaved form, its small glossy leaflets recalling myrtle on slender drooping branches armed with strong hooked spines. The five whitish petals soon flush red in sunlight, and the elliptical fruit ripens red then blackens.
proposals.imageObservation: An arching, sparsely leafed rose with small narrow leaflets and slender drooping branches carrying hooked prickles; four white five-petalled flowers, two open flat around yellow stamens and two still cupped. No fruit is shown.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Small myrtle-like leaflets, drooping branches, hooked prickles and white five-petalled flowers all match. The two claims that cannot be checked from the plate - petals flushing red in sunlight, and elliptical fruit ripening red then blackening - are species/text claims of the kind Thory supplies; c82.net was unreachable so they are unverified rather than unsupported. No contradiction with the image.

proposals.title: Rosa Sempervirens Leschenaultiana
proposals.currentDescription: A variety of Rosa sempervirens named for the traveller Leschenault, who found it on a high mountain in southern Asia; its violet branches and foliage carry a glaucous bloom like hoarfrost. Large pure-white heart-notched petals surround many stamens and a bristled column of fused styles topped with violet stigmas.
proposals.imageObservation: A single large white five-petalled rose with a broad boss of yellow stamens at the top of a notably glaucous, violet-grey stem, with dark green, glossy pinnate leaflets.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The glaucous violet stems the description leads with are clearly visible, and Rosa leschenaultiana is indeed a south Indian (Nilgiri) species collected by Leschenault, so the naming story is consistent. The 'bristled column of fused styles topped with violet stigmas' is below what this reproduction resolves - I could not confirm or refute it; the visible centre reads yellow.

proposals.title: Rosa Spinulifolia
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa spinulifolia, a shrub with red-brown branches bearing long straight solitary spines and leaflets set beneath with many small hooked prickles along the veins. The single soft-pink flowers stand at the branch tips on bristly glandular stalks, with the styles free.

issues.quote: The single soft-pink flowers
issues.problem: The flowers read white with a pink blush rather than pink; a defensible reading, but at the edge.
issues.evidence: image

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: a long red-brown cane armed with widely spaced, long straight spines runs diagonally across the sheet; two open five-petalled flowers, white with a pink blush and yellow stamens, sit at the tips of leafy side shoots; a single detached leaflet is drawn at lower left. White ground.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Red-brown branches, long straight solitary spines, single flowers at the shoot tips and glandular-bristly stalks are all visible and correct. Two claims are botanical-text detail I cannot settle from the reproduction and did not flag as wrong: the hooked prickles on the leaf undersides along the veins (there is one detached leaflet at lower left, presumably drawn for that purpose, but the detail is below the resolution here) and 'the styles free'. c82.net, which carries Thory's text, returns 403.

proposals.title: Rosa Stylosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa stylosa, the field rose, a shrub with twisting greyish branches and serrated glossy leaflets, its soft-pink flowers borne several together and whitening quickly in sun. The styles fuse into a short column, as in Rosa arvensis, and the elliptical hip ripens red.

issues.quote: the field rose
issues.problem: Rosa stylosa's usual English name is the short-styled field rose; 'the field rose' on its own is normally Rosa arvensis, which the same sentence then names as a comparison.
issues.evidence: knowledge | standard British vernacular names

proposals.imageObservation: Botanical plate: three open five-petalled pale pink roses with yellow stamens, several buds, and serrated green leaflets on greyish-brown branches with scattered prickles. No hip is shown.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The united column of styles is the diagnostic character of R. stylosa and is correctly tied to R. arvensis. The red elliptical hip is a species character described from botany, not from this plate (no hip is shown), which is legitimate context rather than a claim about the image. Kept accurate; the common-name looseness is a nit.

proposals.title: Rosa Sulfurea
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa sulfurea, the sulphur-yellow rose, its stem set with fine yellowish subulate spines and seven-leaflet wings, the solitary scentless flowers a pale yellow on short smooth stalks. Among its earlier illustrators were Clusius, Besler and Andrews, listed in Thory's text.
proposals.imageObservation: A plate of the double sulphur rose: two large, many-petalled yellow blooms and a bud on stems with compound grey-green leaves of five to seven oval leaflets, the thicker lower stem carrying a few prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: I checked the description against Thory's text for this plate via search: it confirms numerous fine yellowish thorns of unequal length, leaves winged with seven oval leaflets, and 'solitary, odorless flowers... pale yellow and carried on short, smooth flower stalks', plus the iconographers Clusius, Besler (Hortus Eystettensis) and Andrews. Every clause in the description tracks that text. The one thing the description omits is that the flowers are conspicuously double, which is the plate's most striking feature - an omission, not an error.

proposals.title: Rosa Tomentosa
proposals.currentDescription: A many-petalled form of Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, with its softly haired leaflets and full pink flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
proposals.imageObservation: One open pink flower with more than a single rank of petals around a ring of yellow stamens, several buds and two spent flowers going to seed, downy grey-green leaflets and a stout stem with red-based prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: 'Many-petalled' matches the plate's own epithet flore multiplici and the semi-double bloom shown; the downy leaflets are visible. The technical sentence (colour-printed stipple engraving from a single plate, finished by hand) is the standard, well-documented process for Les Roses and is not contradicted by anything here — note only that this particular file is Nicholas Rougeux's digital restoration, so the sentence describes the original impression rather than the file.

proposals.title: Rosa Turbinata
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa turbinata, the Frankfort rose, a shrub whose calyx tube narrows and swells into the shape of a spinning top, below tomentose leaflets and sweet-scented double flowers in small corymbs. The young flower stalks bristle with stiff glandular hairs.
proposals.imageObservation: A pinkish-purple double rose seen face-on, a spent flower showing only a mass of yellow stamens, three or four buds on clearly top-shaped (turbinate) green receptacles whose sepals carry fine bristles, and large soft green leaflets below.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The turbinate receptacle that gives the rose its name is plainly visible, as are bristles on the sepals and flower stalks, so the description's distinguishing details match the plate. 'Frankfort rose' is the standard vernacular for Rosa turbinata. The fragrance and 'tomentose' claims come from the (unreachable) c82.net text and cannot be checked from a reproduction.

proposals.title: Rosa Ventenatiana
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa ventenatiana, a low briar with crowded straight prickles whose upper leaves persist around the bud so the open flower seems to rest on a bed of leaves. The fragrant blooms carry four or five ranks of soft-pink petals yellowish toward the claw, above a thimble-shaped calyx tube.
proposals.imageObservation: A pale pink double rose sitting low among its own leaves, with one bud above, on canes densely covered in fine straight prickles.
proposals.reviewerNotes: The distinctive feature the description leads with - upper leaves crowding round so the flower seems to rest on a bed of foliage - is exactly what the plate shows, as are the crowded straight prickles. Fragrance and the calyx-tube shape cannot be judged from the image; they read as Thory paraphrase.

proposals.title: Rosa Villosa
proposals.currentDescription: Rosa villosa, the soft-haired apple rose, known by the grey down on its leaflets and the large bristly hips that earned it the name Rosier a Pommes. Its lightly scented flowers carry five heart-notched petals, light red in cultivated plants and dirty white in wild ones.
proposals.imageObservation: A single pale-pink five-petalled rose with notched petals and a yellow boss of stamens at the top of the stem, one bud beside it, grey-green downy leaflets, small red prickles, and a large bristly orange-red hip with persistent sepals shown separately at the lower right.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Every visual claim — five heart-notched petals, grey down on the leaflets, the large bristly hip — is confirmed by the plate. 'Rosier à pommes' (apple rose) for Rosa villosa is standard. The wild/cultivated colour contrast is Thory's text and unverifiable here, but hedged appropriately.

proposals.title: Rosa Villosa Evrathiana
proposals.currentDescription: A vigorous variety of Rosa villosa reaching ten feet, nearly spineless, with very large dark-green leaflets and flowers hung in a pendent panicle on bristly glandular stalks. The buds open rarely, and those that do show seven or eight ranks of soft-pink petals.

issues.quote: reaching ten feet
issues.problem: Height is not in the record and cannot be read from the plate.
issues.evidence: sourceEvidence — c82.net unreachable.

proposals.imageObservation: A spray of eight or nine unopened pink buds on long bristly, glandular stalks with leafy sepals, above two large compound leaves of very big dark-green leaflets; the stem carries fine bristles but no substantial prickles. Not one flower is open.
proposals.reviewerNotes: Unusually, the description and the plate agree on the odd part: 'The buds open rarely' matches a sheet on which every single flower is still closed, and the near-spineless stems, very large dark leaflets and bristly glandular stalks are all visible. The petal-rank count for the rare open flower cannot be checked against this plate, and neither can the height; both are the sort of detail Thory supplies. I did not lower the verdict for them.
